I share the flat with Yash, so I was there, reading on the sofa, the Sunday he and Nandita finally had the big talk. I pretended not to listen. I failed.

They'd made a list. Actual paper. Where to live: she wants Pune, he wants to stay near his parents in Nashik. Kids: she wants two, he'd said "someday" for a year and now said "one, maybe." Her job abroad offer. His mother's expectation that they'd live with her.

It got tense twice. Once Nandita said, "Don't say 'we'll see.' You always say 'we'll see.'" Yash went red, then said, "Okay. Honestly? I don't want to live with my mother either."

They didn't solve everything. But when she left, they were both smiling, tired. Yash told me later, "Better we fight about this now than after the wedding cards are printed."

— Sahil

The night before our families met to fix the engagement date, I made a list. Not a pros-and-cons list. A list of Anand's flaws.

He is late to everything. He goes quiet when he's upset instead of saying it. He's hopeless with money and spends it on books.

Then I made another list, underneath. How he handles the flaws. When he's late, he says sorry and doesn't make excuses. When he goes quiet, he comes back within a day and tells me what was wrong. When we fought about his mother last year, he listened, and then he actually changed something.

I looked at the two lists for a long time. I wasn't swept off my feet. I haven't been since the first months. What I felt was steadier: I respect how he handles trouble.

So the next day, when my father asked, "Are you sure?", I said yes and meant it.

— Bidisha

Premarital session note, final session

Thomas and Ruth attended their fourth and last session before their wedding in April.

In earlier sessions they had argued about money and about Ruth's long hours. Today they described a fight from last month over his sister's visit. Ruth said, "He shut down, like always. Then he came back two hours later and said, 'I was scared of disappointing her. Can we plan it together?'" Thomas added, "And she didn't hold it against me."

When I asked what they valued most in each other, neither said "passion." Thomas said, "She's fair." Ruth said, "He comes back."

They are not starry-eyed. They know each other's weak spots. What I observe is respect, and trust in their repair.

I closed our sessions by suggesting they return if a pattern gets stuck.

— Vishal, counsellor

Nakul proposed today. Properly. In the park near Amma's house, with Lakshmi aunty's dog barking the whole time.

I said yes. And I'm writing this down because I want to remember why.

It wasn't fireworks. The fireworks were in the first year, and honestly, they faded. What I have now is different. I know he snores and sulks when he loses at carrom. He knows I get snappy when I'm hungry and I never admit I'm wrong on the first try.

But last winter, when I lost my job, he didn't try to fix me. He sat with me. And when we fight, we come back to it. Every time. We say, "Okay, what really happened?"

I admire him. I trust us. That's what I said yes to.

Not a feeling. A decision, with open eyes.

— Arohi

We met at the inter-school debate. After that we'd video call till two in the morning. I'd fall asleep in first period. My mother kept asking why I looked like a ghost.

My half-yearly marks dropped in two subjects. Sunaina's too. We joked about it. It didn't feel like a problem. It felt like we were the only two people in the world and everything else was background noise.

He'd thought about texting. It would have been easier. But Nazia deserved to see his face.

"Nazia, I need to tell you something. I don't feel the same anymore. I've been thinking about it for a while, and I don't want to keep pretending or give you false hope."

"I'm sorry. I really liked what we had."

Walking home, he felt terrible, and also sure he'd done it the right way.

Gautam bhaiya,

You asked me how I ended it with Shalini, since you said I'd been avoiding it for weeks. I finally did it on Sunday.

I didn't text. I called her. I'd written down what I wanted to say so I wouldn't ramble: "Shalini, I don't feel the same anymore, and I don't want to mislead you. I'm really sorry."

She was quiet. Then she asked if she'd done something wrong. I said no, and that I didn't want to list reasons that would only hurt. I didn't say "maybe later" or "let's stay close," because I didn't mean them.

The call was eleven minutes. I felt awful afterwards. I sat on the terrace for an hour.

But I think I did it with respect. She deserved a real answer, not months of me going quiet.

Kishore

You asked how I ended it with Hafsa. I'm Imran, and I'll be honest: it was the hardest phone call of my life.

We'd been together since the start of Class 11. By the end of the year, I knew I didn't feel the same. I delayed for weeks. Then I realised every day I waited, she was still planning things for us.

So I called her. Not a text. I said, "Hafsa, I care about you, but I don't feel the same anymore, and I don't want to mislead you." I didn't list her flaws. I didn't say "maybe someday."

She cried. I wanted to take it back, just to stop her crying. But I didn't. That would have been worse.

A month later she told her friend, and her friend told me, that she was glad I was clear. It still hurt her. But she didn't have to wonder.

Leela had ended it on Sunday, kindly, by the temple tank. By Wednesday, Tanvir still felt as if someone had scooped out his chest.

He checked her profile forty times a day. Her new photo from the Dussehra mela, smiling with her cousins. Every smile felt aimed at him.

On Wednesday night he typed a post about "people who pretend to care." His thumb hovered over Share.

His older brother, Faiz, came onto the roof where Tanvir was sitting. He saw the phone and didn't grab it. He just sat down.

"You want to post that?"

"She's acting like nothing happened."

"Maybe. Or maybe she's sad too and hiding it. Either way, that post will follow you around this whole small town."

Tanvir deleted it. Then, without meaning to, he started crying. Faiz stayed. Later he said, "It's this bad because it mattered. It won't stay this bad."

Three days after Mats broke up with her, Ulla was still checking his photos in her Stockholm bedroom. He had gone skating with his friends on Saturday, as if nothing had happened. Her chest felt hollow, like a room with the furniture taken out.

She drafted a post, a song lyric about liars. She wanted him to see it.

Xin, her best friend, turned up with cinnamon buns and a blanket. She read the draft over Ulla's shoulder.

"You can post it," Xin said. "But in a week you'll be embarrassed, and he'll show it to everyone."

Ulla closed the app. Then she cried into the blanket for ten minutes, and Xin didn't say anything, just passed tissues.

Later Ulla told her mother everything over dinner. Her mother said, "It hurts this much because you cared. It will get smaller. Not today, but it will."

Samir and I have been together six years. We have a rhythm. I make the coffee, he does the dishes. Sunday is biryani and a film. We finish each other's grocery lists.

I love it. It's safe.

But last month, at a friend's wedding, someone asked Samir what he was reading these days, and he talked for ten minutes about a book on the history of trains. I'd never heard him mention it. I didn't know he liked trains.

On the drive home I asked him, "When did you start that book?"

"Two months ago," he said. "You were busy with your exams."

It wasn't a fight. We laughed about it. But I kept thinking: what else have I stopped asking about? When did the comfort turn into not knowing?

I've started asking him one real question every evening. It feels awkward. It also feels necessary.

— Chetan

Sahil and Manjula have come every Saturday for a year. They told me they've been together six years. They're easy with each other: she fixes his collar without thinking, he knows exactly when she'll turn.

Today I paired everyone with new partners for one song. Manjula danced with a younger man who asked her questions the whole time: where she grew up, what she likes about dancing. She laughed more in three minutes than I'd seen all year.

Sahil noticed. When they came back together, he asked her, half joking, "What were you two talking about?"

"He asked what I like about salsa," she said. "Nobody's asked me that in a long time."

Sahil looked at her for a second longer than usual. After class, I saw them sitting on the steps, talking, not dancing.

— Ines, instructor

The Singapore offer is real. They want an answer by the 15th. I want to go. I've wanted something like this since college.

I know you want to stay in Jaipur, near your parents. I know your father's health is on your mind, and that you love our small life here: the Sunday market, your cricket, our balcony.

Vidya

"We should talk about it," she said at last.

"Later," he said. "After your exams are marked."
